cards.title: Mohan, Haderle, Lindsay, Pirahesh and Schwarz
cards.sub: 1992 · IBM Almaden Research Center and Santa Teresa Laboratory, San Jose
cards.prompt: Before ARIES, what were these five actually spending their time on, and what did it turn up in code that had already shipped to customers?
cards.answer: Reading the thin documentation and the source of System R, SQL/DS, DB2/MVS and IMS to work out how each one's recovery really behaved. It turned up significant design bugs in System R roughly ten years after its product version, SQL/DS, was released.
cards.body: Four at Almaden, Don Haderle at IBM's Santa Teresa lab across town. Not a clean-sheet team: archaeologists in IBM's own transaction code. Mohan later wrote that most of them had not been IBMers during the System R days, which let them look with a fresh perspective.

cards.title: The undo that undid nothing
cards.sub: Figure 16 of the 1992 paper · selective redo meets record-level locking
cards.prompt: A page takes update 20 from a transaction that will be rolled back, then update 30 from one that commits. Selective redo replays only 30. What breaks when the undo pass reaches 20?
cards.answer: Redoing 30 pushed that page's LSN past 20. Undo decides by comparing the page's LSN against the log record's, so it undoes update 20 — which the page never received. The paper's figure labels the outcome ERROR?!
cards.body: No outage and no price tag: a latent correctness hole in recovery code that had shipped. The authors' fix is not a smarter rule but abandoning selectivity, and they note that running undo before redo does not rescue it. Skip one record and a page's position stops describing the page.

cards.title: ARIES: A Transaction Recovery Method Supporting Fine-Granularity Locking and Partial Rollbacks Using Write-Ahead Logging
cards.sub: Mohan, Haderle, Lindsay, Pirahesh, Schwarz · ACM TODS 17(1), March 1992
cards.prompt: Open the paper. During the redo pass, which updates get replayed, and what single comparison decides whether any one of them is actually applied to a page?
cards.answer: All of them, including updates by transactions already known to be losers. An update is redone only if the affected page's page-LSN is less than the log record's LSN, and no logging is performed while redoing — so replay is idempotent by arithmetic.
cards.body: ACM Transactions on Database Systems 17(1), March 1992, pages 94-162 — the range is printed on the paper's own first page, not borrowed from an index. Section 1 states the rule the rest rests on: log records for a change must be on stable storage before the changed page may overwrite its old version.

cards.title: Every derived store that carries an offset
cards.sub: Mohan's VLDB 1999 retrospective · the implementation list
cards.prompt: Name two things on Mohan's 1999 list of ARIES implementations that are not databases, and say what a Kafka consumer's committed offset is the same object as.
cards.answer: The NT file system and MQSeries, IBM's messaging and queuing product; Encina's recoverable file system counts too. A committed offset is a page-LSN — a derived store recording its own position in the log, so a restart replays exactly the suffix it is missing.
cards.body: The list runs past databases into a file system and a message queue, because the shape is not a database trick. Kafka makes the move once more and keeps the positions in a log of their own: __consumer_offsets, compacted to the latest value per key.
